entries.title: ICC unseals Taliban leaders' warrants over persecuting women
entries.summary: The court gave more details on the warrants for four Taliban leaders accused of the crime against humanity of gender persecution of women, girls and the LGBTQ+ community. The Islamist group rejected the warrants.
entries.content:
October 5, 2026

The court gave more details on the warrants for four Taliban leaders accused of the crime against humanity of gender persecution of women, girls and the LGBTQ+ community. The Islamist group rejected the warrants.

The International Criminal Court (ICC) disclosed on Monday more details about the arrest warrants against two Taliban leaders, while also issuing two more arrest warrants.

The four Taliban leaders are accused of crimes against humanity through the persecution of women, girls and the LGBTQ+ community in  Afghanistan since taking power in 2021.

According to the court, warrants were issued in July and September of last year against Hibatullah Akhundzada , the Taliban's Supreme Leader, as well as against Abdul Hakim Haqqani, who heads the country's Supreme Court.

The other two warrants were issued against Education Minister Habibullah Agha and Minister of Higher Education Neda Mohammad Nadim.

The four are charged with persecution on grounds of gender of "girls, women and other persons nonconforming with the Taliban's policy on gender, gender identity or expression; and on political grounds against persons perceived as 'allies of girls and women,'" according to the court.

What does the ICC accuse the 4 Taliban leaders of?

The judges who issued the warrants said that the four implemented policies that saw "severe violations of fundamental rights and freedoms of the civilian population of Afghanistan, in connection with conducts of murder, imprisonment, torture, rape and enforced disappearance."

The Taliban "specifically targeted girls and women by reason of their gender," the judges added, also mentioning persecution against people due to "certain expressions of sexuality and/or gender identity."

The ICC has no jurisdiction to execute the warrants. Still, the move is considered a form of pressure on the Afghan ruling authority.

The Taliban have taken a wide range of measures to restrict women's access to jobs and education beyond sixth grade, as well as barring them from most public spaces.

Women are also obligated to cover their whole bodies apart from their eyes upon leaving home, with a male relative having to accompany them on long trips.

Taliban rejects ICC's warrants

Afghanistan's government spokesperson said the country does not recognize the court's authority.

"We are bound by the rulings of Islamic Sharia and its courts, not by intelligence entities or so-called courts." chief spokesman Zabihullah Mujahid said in a statement.

A request for warrants for Akhundzada and Haqqani made last year by former ICC chief prosecutor Karim Khan argued that "Afghan women and girls as well as the LGBTQI+ community are facing an unprecedented, unconscionable and ongoing persecution by the Taliban.”

The UN Human Rights Council has called on the Taliban to drop its "systematic oppression of all women and girls in Afghanistan."

Human rights groups have been calling for the international community to do more against the Taliban's gender-based policies in Afghanistan.

Edited by: Rana Taha

entries.title: Australia's migrant policy offers lessons for EU and US
entries.summary: Australia has used offshore processing centers to deter asylum seekers for more than two decades. As the EU and US pursue similar third-country arrangements, Australia's experience highlights the potential problems.
entries.content:
October 5, 2026

Australia has used offshore processing centers to deter asylum seekers for more than two decades. As the EU and US pursue similar third-country arrangements, Australia's experience highlights the potential problems.

Nations that send asylum seekers to third countries for offshore processing and holding could spend billions, only to face accusations of human rights abuses and financial mismanagement, as in Australia.

The European Union (EU) has nevertheless been considering the idea, and the United States (US) has already made similar third-country deals, but Australia has been processing or relocating people outside the country where they seek protection for more than two decades.

Former Australian Prime Minister John Howard introduced the so-called "Pacific Solution" in 2001, targeting immigrants who arrived by boat, and establishing Australian migration processing centers with the help from governments in Papua New Guinea (PNG) and the tiny island nation of Nauru .

Thousands sent to islands under Australia's 'Pacific Solution'

Center-left and center-right governments described the policy as a deterrent, saying people were less likely to attempt dangerous ocean crossings or pay smugglers if arriving by boat did not provide a route to Australia. In his 2001 election policy speech, Howard said the famous line, frequently quoted since: "We will decide who comes to this country and the circumstances in which they come."

In 2008, a newly elected Labor Party government phased out the practice, saying it was a cynical, costly, and ultimately unsuccessful exercise.

But faced with more deaths at sea, a Labor government under Prime Minister Julia Gillard started sending maritime arrivals to Nauru and Manus again in 2012, after an expert panel recommended reopening the centers.

"I'm not going to play politics or look at political scoreboards when too many lives have been lost," Gillard said at the time.

Between 2013 and 2014, the number of people transferred offshore peaked to more than 3,000.

Journalists have been mostly barred from the centers on Nauru and Manus Island. Graham Thom, Advocacy Coordinator for the Refugee Council of Australia (RCOA), told DW that this lack of access and independent oversight meant many Australians accepted the narrative that the policy was working.

EU considers offshore arrangements

People without a legal right to remain in the EU could face deportation to third countries as soon as 2027, with Rwanda and Uzbekistan reportedly under consideration as third-party countries, as well as Uganda.

The European Parliament in June approved new rules that would pave the way for so-called "return hubs" outside the EU's borders.

Denmark's Minister for Immigration and Integration, Morten Bodskov, told reporters last month the hubs would not be detention and deportation centers.

"We are not talking about camps," Bodskov said, describing the scheme instead as "a new chance to have a life in a partner country."

Denmark, alongside Germany, Austria, Greece, and the Netherlands, known collectively as the Group of Five, said in September they had agreed on steps towards a deal with a non-EU country, without naming it.

The group was to speak with the United Nations (UN) body, the International Organization for Migration, and the UN Refugee Agency about their next steps.

The proposal allows for harsh penalties for those who refuse to be removed to the hubs, including detention for up to 30 months pending deportation from the EU and entry bans.

US already has a third country migration scheme

The US government has already made deals with at least 30 third countries in Africa and Latin America. In June, Amnesty International said some agreements had been revealed through the US Freedom of Information Act, while others "remain secret."

The US Supreme Court ruled late last month that the second Trump administration could resume deportations under the third-country scheme, after a US appeals court ruled that immigrants must receive effective notice of their intended destination and an opportunity to challenge removal if they fear persecution or torture.

The first deportations from the US under the third-country removal scheme were of immigrants convicted of crimes, but more recently, foreign nationals not accused of any crime have also been deported. 

Accusations of human rights abuse

Asylum seekers and human rights advocates have repeatedly alleged human rights abuses in Australia's offshore migration processing program, with Thom describing the policy as a "medieval idea."

A group of asylum seekers formerly detained on Manus Island reached a AU$70 million (€43.47 million/$48.47 million) settlement in 2017 after filing charges for abuse and unlawful detention.

In February, an Australian Senate inquiry heard first-hand witness accounts of neglect, untreated health conditions, and serious concerns for the safety and dignity of camps inhabitants — especially of women being kept on Nauru. Prior to the hearing, 73 UN member states had publicly raised concerns about Australia's migration policies.

Brazil, China, Finland, Germany, Serbia, Switzerland and Turkey called for an end to offshore processing of asylum claims.

Australia has yet to officially comment on the recommendations, but successive governments have said offshore processing helps deter dangerous boat journeys, with former Prime Minister Tony Abbott describing the policy during his term as "decent, humane and compassionate."

The effect of offshore processing is difficult to isolate from other policy measures, especially the practice of turning back asylum boats. This "turnback" policy was introduced and reintroduced under conservative governments in 2001 and 2013 respectively, but with inconsistent data on incidents.

As in the US, offshore migration processing for Australia has expanded beyond its original scope, with Nauru recently agreeing to accept convicted foreign nationals from Australia who can't legally be returned to their countries of origin, at a cost of AU$2.5 billion over the next 30 years. Australia had already spent more than AU$13 billion on offshore detention since 2012.

Measuring the success of Australia's model is difficult, but its significant long-term costs and legal and human rights concerns may serve as a warning for other countries considering similar policies.

Edited by: Andreas Illmer

entries.title: Yemen launches major military operation against Houthis
entries.summary: Yemen's internationally recognized government has launched a new military offensive to retake Houthi-held territory, as the Iran-backed rebel group claims new attacks in Saudi Arabia.
entries.content:
Yemen

Yemen launches major military operation against Houthis

October 5, 2026

Yemen's internationally recognized government has launched a new military offensive to retake Houthi-held territory, as the Iran-backed rebel group claims new attacks in Saudi Arabia.

Yemen's military and a Saudi-led coalition launched an offensive against Iran-backed Houthi fighters on Monday, a day after Yemeni Presidential Council chief Rashad al-Alimi announced the lofty goal of retaking all territory held by the Iran-backed rebel group.  

The Yemeni military said Monday operations were commencing in the Houthi-held capital, Sanaa, while the Saudi-led coalition said it had hit Houthi "military targets" in the town of Hodeida on the Red Sea coast.

A coalition spokesman on X said that naval forces had "destroyed weapons depots, facilities storing booby-trapped boats and naval mines" and had "thwarted a planned attack" targeting waterways in the southern Red Sea.

Yemeni officials said forces allied with the internationally recognized government retook the crucial town of Dhubab just north of strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait.

Sunday's announcement came after Houthi fighters captured a key road linking the key southwestern city of Taiz with the government-held city of Aden, effectively isolating Taiz. The rebels have besieged Taiz for more than a decade.

More than 70 people were reportedly killed in fighting around Taiz over the past day, according to AFP news agency.

Houthi's claim new strikes on Riyadh

Meanwhile, a Houthi military spokesman said Monday that ballistic missiles and drones targeted King Khalid International Airport in the Saudi capital, Riyadh, and an oil refinery in the Red Sea city of Rabigh.

The spokesman said the Aramco refinery in Rabigh was also hit along with military sites and smaller airports in the south.

There was no immediate confirmation from Saudi authorities on the reported strikes.

Mecca alliance to deploy forces

In response to the latest escalation, Turkey, and Pakistan agreed on Monday to deploy troops as part of the collective defense agreement under the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement the two countries signed in August with Saudi Arabia.

The move came after an emergency meeting in Riyadh.

In a joint statement, the trio "reaffirmed their unequivocal rejection of any attack or threat against the Kingdom's security and territorial integrity."

The statement did not specify what sort of role the troops would fill once in Saudi Arabia.

The three countries condemned the Houthis' targeting of Saudi Arabia's two holiest cities, Mecca and Medina, as well as agreeing to provide the "agreed military forces and capabilities," which will be deployed in Saudi Arabia.

How did the conflict between Saudi Arabia and Houthis escalate?

The latest developments come amid an escalation between the Houthis and the internationally recognized government in Yemen that is supported by Saudi Arabia, reviving Yemen's civil war after a four-year ceasefire.

A 2022 truce between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia collapsed in July after the rebels allowed an Iranian plane to land in Yemen's capital Sanaa, which defied the Saudis' control over Yemeni airspace.

As a result of the escalation, the Houthis announced a maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia.

Last month, the Houthis seized Yemen's Red Sea coast and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait — a vital global shipping route — from government hands, even as Al-Alimi called for support from the international community.

At the same time, Houthi's have been launching long-range attacks at targets in Saudi Arabia.

The Iran-backed Houthis have controlled Sanaa and much of Yemen's more populous western areas since the start of Yemen's civil war in 2014.

Edited by: Elizabeth Schumacher and Wesley Dockery

entries.title: Denmark: Data of millions compromised in hack
entries.summary: The breach by the hackers was through the legitimate login credentials of a local company, initial findings suggest. The data of some 8.8 million registered people was compromised.
entries.content:
October 5, 2026

The breach by the hackers was through the legitimate login credentials of a local company, initial findings suggest. The data of some 8.8 million registered people was compromised.

Denmark's national registry was hacked in an incident the authorities described as "extremely serious."

Hackers secured access to personal information on millions of people, the country's digital affairs ministry said on Monday. The compromised information included names, addresses and social security numbers, known in Denmark as national registry numbers.

The data of some 8.8 million registered people was compromised. This figure exceeds Denmark's population size because it includes people who have already died or emigrated, the Danish authorities said in a statement.

The breach by the hackers was through the legitimate login credentials of a local company, initial findings suggest. The hackers have not yet been identified. The means they used to gain access has since been cut off.

The ministry said it was first alerted to an "anomaly" in the system "during September."

Information of deceased, emigrated people included

Denmark has a population of roughly six million people. However, its national registry includes information of eleven million people, which includes the data of those deceased or people who have moved abroad and don't live in Denmark anymore.

Christina Egelund, Denmark's digital affairs minister, said the incident's full extent will investigated by the authorities.

"This is an extremely serious incident," Egelund said. "We are in the process of tracking the exact extent of this incident with all those affected."

Danish news agency Ritzau reported that the register includes information on church membership, details of legal incapacitation and restrictions on legal capacity.

Edited by: Wesley Dockery

entries.title: Merz, Macron seek tougher EU measures against unfair trade
entries.summary: Emmanuel Macron and Friedrich Merz have written to Ursula von der Leyen, calling for tougher EU mechanisms against unfair trade practices by other states. They name no names but seem to have China or the US in mind.
entries.content:
October 5, 2026

Emmanuel Macron and Friedrich Merz have written to Ursula von der Leyen, calling for tougher EU mechanisms against unfair trade practices by other states. They name no names but seem to have China or the US in mind.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron sent a joint appeal to the European Commission on Monday, calling for tougher EU measures against unfair trade practices by other states. 

They said that the existing instruments at the EU's disposal were no longer sufficient.

The appeal did not name any specific country but it seemed most clearly tied to Chinese trade policy, the EU's vast deficit with China, and its dependence on certain key raw materials. The other apparent candidate would be the US, not least under the current unpredictable trade policy stewardship of tariff-loving President Donald Trump.

It also came just a few days before the EU's trade commissioner, Maros Sefcovic, is set to visit Beijing.

What did Merz and Macron say?

The joint letter to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called for two new measures to be introduced in Brussels. 

One would aim at ensuring diversification and preventing companies from becoming too dependent on suppliers from individual companies.

The other would allow another country to be excluded from access to the European single market on an expedited basis if exceptional circumstances made this necessary.

Merz and Macron wrote that this could be used in cases "where third countries deliberately seek to undermine the restoration of a level playing field and fair market conditions through political or economic means, leading to serious and systematic distortions of our single market."

The French and German leaders, both struggling to balance economic growth and public spending, said the EU's struggles to maintain global competitiveness and its dependencies on certain suppliers of core materials led to "geoeconomic risks."

"The open and rules-based trading system is being massively compromised by the instrumentalization of trade, systemic market-distorting practices and global macroeconomic imbalances," they wrote. "All this undermines the level competitive playing field for our companies, our position as a sovereign core industrial producer and our capacity for innovations, which leads to increasing dependencies and geoeconomic risks."

Appeal comes ahead of EU China visit, and EU leaders' summit

Monday's letter is what's known in EU diplomatic circles as a "non-paper." These are nonbinding, informal documents shared between EU member states and institutions that are supposed to propose ideas and initiate discussions without officially committing to a position.

It recommends authorizing the Commission to exclude a country from single market access in extreme situations if it sees the need — currently a complicated process that would take some time to arrange and requires approval from member states.

It suggests reversing this process: allowing the Commission to take the step independently, but with member states then having the chance to block it with a qualified majority vote, which the EU currently defines as a vote by a minimum of 55% of member states that also represents a minimum of 65% of the bloc's total population.

The EU's trade deficit with China is vast and growing. The EU put the figure at around €360 billion (roughly $400 billion) in 2025, though China's statisticians reached a more modest tally of $292 billion.

The bloc is also particularly dependent on China for a number of raw materials, not least rare earths, and is increasingly reliant on both the US and China for high-tech imports and services, particularly in computing and the so-called AI sector. 

The EU's trade commissioner, Maros Sefcovic, visits China this week for talks, ahead of an EU leaders' summit next week, on October 15-16. Sefcovic said earlier this year that he hoped to see "tangible results by October" on the question of trade with China, although whether these will materialize is an open question.

Beijing has warned that it could retaliate with changes of its own after learning of the EU's plans, if it perceives a need to.

Edited by: Wesley Dockery

entries.title: Ukraine says Russian drones behind Turkish ship sinking
entries.summary: Romanian authorities did not say what caused the fire, but local media reported that the ship was carrying grain and was hit by a drone.
entries.content:
Romania

Ukraine says Russian drones behind Turkish ship sinking

October 5, 2026

Romanian authorities did not say what caused the fire, but local media reported that the ship was carrying grain and was hit by a drone.

Romanian authorities said on Monday that two people were killed and another one was wounded after a fire broke out in a commercial vessel on Romanian waters in the Black Sea.

The Turkish-owned civilian vessel subsequently sank. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the incident was caused by a Russian drone attack.

Romania's Interior Ministry said the Coast Guard was alerted at around 11 a.m. local time (14:00 UTC) and the afflicted vessel was in Romania's exclusive economic zone, some 30 nautical miles (55 kilometers) south of Sfantul Gheorghe in Tulcea County.

"Eleven crew members have been rescued. Two deceased individuals have also been located," the ministry said, adding that a helicopter had airlifted the injured.

Zelenskyy accuses Russia of 'horrific strike'

Authorities did not identify the cause of the fire, but Romanian media reported that the ship was carrying grain and was hit by a drone.

"A ‌horrific strike by two Russian drones on ‌a civilian vessel in neutral ‌waters carrying corn and owned by Türkiye. Azerbaijani and Indian citizens were on board," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy wrote on X.

"As ⁠of now, unfortunately, we know that the ship's captain was ‌killed ... The fate of one other ⁠person is still being established," he added.

The Ukrainian government says it has repeatedly proposed taking steps to de-escalate the situation in the Black Sea, which is putting maritime trade at risk.

"But Russia consistently chooses terror and sinking civilian vessels instead of normal maritime navigation," Zelenskyy wrote on social media.

Rising threat to Black Sea maritime traffic

The Black Sea is a major commercial shipping route, which connects Ukraine's grain exports with the rest of the world. The waterway has faced heightened security concerns since Russia launched its full-scale war on Ukraine in 2022.

There has been an increase in war-related objects found in the Black Sea, mostly in Romanian, Bulgarian and Turkish waters, with analysts saying the trend is expected to continue.

The incident is the latest to take place on Romanian waters. In August, a Romanian F-16 fighter jet destroyed a marine drone near an offshore gas project in the Black Sea.

Two months before, a Ukrainian maritime drone exploded in Romania's Black Sea port of Constanta, with Ukraine saying the drone had been knocked off course by Russian electronic interference.

Edited by: Wesley Dockery

entries.title: Australia, New Zealand probe Flydubai pilot's time there
entries.summary: The Flydubai pilot from Oman suspected of trying to crash a plane in Israel spent time in Oceania as a young man. Police in both Australia and New Zealand said they would investigate his links to the countries.
entries.content:
Israel

Australia, New Zealand probe Flydubai pilot's time there

October 5, 2026

The Flydubai pilot from Oman suspected of trying to crash a plane in Israel spent time in Oceania as a young man. Police in both Australia and New Zealand said they would investigate his links to the countries.

Security agencies in Australia and New Zealand on Monday said they were investigating the time that the co-pilot of Flydubai flight FZ1073 spent in the countries in his youth 

The Omani national is in custody in the United Arab Emirates. He is suspected of attacking his pilot Smit Machchhar with the emergency ax in the cockpit, and attempting to hijack the plane and crash it intentionally in Israel. 

The pilot and passengers combined to thwart his attempts and restrain him. After a near-vertical dive lasting around 30 seconds during the fight for control, the plane made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.

What did Australian and New Zealand authorities say about the case?

The Royal Melbourne Institute of Technology (RMIT) said on Monday that the man had enrolled at the Melbourne university in the state of Victoria, but said that he did not successfully complete an engineering qualification.

A spokesman for the Australian Federal Police said that the Victorian Counter Terrorism Team — comprising federal poice, Victorian state police, and the ASIO intelligence agency — was "investigating the man's links to Australia."

Based on Australian media reports, the man arrived on an Australian student visa in 2014, enrolled in 2015, left in 2017, and had his visa canceled in 2019.

Similarly, police in New Zealand said on Monday that the suspect spent time there, without specifying exactly where or when.

"We are looking into the time he spent here, alongside other agencies where appropriate," New Zealand Police assistant commissioner Micahel Johnson told the RNZ news outlet, issuing similar comments elsewhere. "We are unable to comment further at this time."

Flight FZ1073's pilot, Indian national Machchhar, also spent some of his formative years in New Zealand. He completed his early flight training some 18 years ago with the Mainland Air carrier. 

"I was really pleased to read how he handled the situation," the airline's chief executive Philip Kean told RNZ. "He got through and he got the door open so the other people could save the airplane, because if he hadn't done that, it would have been a disaster."

Edited by: Wesley Dockery

entries.title: Euro plummets against US dollar: has the next financial crisis begun?
entries.summary: The euro has fallen to a 17-month low against the dollar. That will make inflation worse in the EU, where political worries and concern over French debt are already troubling investors. Is a fiscal crisis at hand?
entries.content:
October 5, 2026

The euro has fallen to a 17-month low against the dollar. That will make inflation worse in the EU, where political worries and concern over French debt are already troubling investors. Is a fiscal crisis at hand?

The euro hit a 17-month low against the dollar in early trading on Monday, as concerns over eurozone debt, particularly in France, compounded existing investor concerns over global government bond yields and rising oil prices.

The euro has been sliding against the dollar for much of 2026, down around 5% since the start of the year. It reached $1.12 on Monday, the lowest level since early in 2025.

Ricardo Amaro, lead eurozone economist with Oxford Economics, told DW that the general slide can be attributed to a repricing of investor expectations regarding US Federal Reserve policy in terms of higher interest rates in the face of rising global bond yields.

However, he said the latest sell-off was prompted in particular by concerns over France, where "investors positioned for higher fiscal risk."

The France problem

The sell-off in French debt gathered pace last week as doubts grow over its long-term viability. French 10-year government bonds — the cost France must pay to borrow money within 10 years of the debt being issued — rose to a 5% yield before easing slightly.

France has long had underlying fiscal problems. Since President Emmanuel Macron came to office in May 2017, public spending has climbed while he has brought in deep tax cuts. As a result, the country's national debt has increased by well over €1 trillion ($1.12 trillion).

France's debt-to-GDP ratio now stands at almost 118%. It consistently posts unbalanced budgets. Its annual budget deficit is now regularly more than 5%, above the 3.4% rate when Macron came to office.

For many investors, wider concerns over low eurozone growth levels and surging energy prices have contributed to a renewed focus on France, with many retreating to perceived safer options, such as German government debt.

The difference between French and German government 10-year debt yields reached their highest level since the eurozone debt crisis last week, a closely-watched measure of EU financial stability.

What can the ECB do?

The resulting pressure on the euro and on other government bond markets, including Italy's, means there are calls for the European Central Bank (ECB) to take action to prevent concern over France turning into panic.

Deutsche Bank's Jim Reid said in a note on Monday that at one point last week, the spread between German and French bonds had become so wide that a "mini-panic" was at hand.

"The big question is whether this is the start of a new euro sovereign crisis or whether markets have already overshot," he said.

Ricardo Amaro said the situation presents a challenge for the ECB because it needs to act without making things worse. "Sounding too hawkish would also add to pressure on France's bond yields, which became an important driver of euro weakness," he added.

He expects policymakers to continue monitoring currency developments between the US dollar and the euro, but to stop short of trying to influence the market for now.

What is at stake?

Uncertainty abounds due to both political and economic pressures. France has been beset by political crises in recent years, where passing annual budgets has become a major test of government stability.

Although the 2027 budget has been agreed, with reforms aimed at reducing the deficit, the right-wing National Rally remains well-placed ahead of the 2027 presidential election, in which Marine Le Pen is likely to be the lead candidate.

Concerns over French economic policy in the event of Le Pen winning the presidency are spooking investors, similar to how the rise of the populist AfD in Germany has raised questions over the future direction of the bloc's key economy.

Much of the political instability has been driven by voter anger over the high cost of living. In Spain, Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has just called a snap election after measures to deal with the country's housing crisis were voted down in parliament.

Amaro says a weakening euro could compound the underlying problem of inflation.

"Sharper euro weakness would reinforce the inflationary shock at a time when inflation is already expected to stay high into 2027," he said.

A weaker euro would increase the cost of imported goods, particularly those that are priced in US dollars. Global commodities such as oil and gas are priced in dollars, meaning soaring energy prices would likely rise further, as would US imports.

The next financial crisis?

With memories of the sovereign debt crisis that afflicted the EU in the early 2010s still fresh, many observers are beginning to wonder if the moves on French debt could be indicative of a new crisis in the eurozone.

Some, such as Geoffrey Yu, a senior strategist with BNY, believes such concerns are misplaced. "Comparisons to 2012 are well off the mark," he said.

However, Amaro says the fact that further interest rate hikes are expected from the ECB this year, combined with the worsening inflation outlook, makes this a situation which needs to be managed and monitored very carefully.

"Euro weakness shouldn't be interpreted as an isolated development," he says. "If triggered by growing concerns about France's fiscal outlook, then the ECB would certainly want to thread that carefully given risks for the eurozone."

Edited by: Kristie Pladson

entries.title: Military aircraft with 32 people on board crashes in southern Nigeria
entries.summary: Rescue teams searched the crash site after the military aircraft went down in southern Nigeria. All 32 people on the plane are confirmed to have died.
entries.content:
Nigeria

Nigeria military plane crashes with 32 on board

October 5, 2026

Rescue teams searched the crash site after the military aircraft went down in southern Nigeria. All 32 people on the plane are confirmed to have died.

A military aircraft carrying 25 passengers and seven crew members crashed in southern Nigeria, authorities said on Monday.

Nigerian President Bola Tinubu later said all 32 people on the plane had died in the crash, extending his "deepest condolences" to the deceased's loved ones.

The aircraft was on a routine mission to Lagos, Nigeria's economic hub, when it crashed in the Igbokoda area of Ondo state, Aviation Minister Festus Keyamo said in a statement.

Wreckage located

Keyamo said the aircraft disappeared from radar at around 9 a.m. local time (7:00 a.m. GMT) and was later found to have crashed about halfway through its journey from Edo state to Lagos.

He said the wreckage had been located near a naval base.

The Nigerian Air Force identified the aircraft as an ATR-42 and said an immediate search and rescue operation had been launched.

A video circulating on social media showed a small crowd gathered near a river as rescuers searched the area by boat.

Locals told AP news agency about what they had heard and seen.

"The plane cleared some trees. We found some body parts, some clothes and shoes," one of the locals said.

Edited by: Wesley Dockery

entries.title: Iran poised to exploit security vacuum as US leaves Iraq
entries.summary: The end of the US military mission in Iraq leaves the Kurdistan region facing a severe security vacuum. As Erbil grapples with deep internal divisions, Tehran is well positioned to make strategic gains.
entries.content:
Iran

Iran poised to exploit security vacuum as US leaves Iraq

October 5, 2026

The end of the US military mission in Iraq leaves the Kurdistan region facing a severe security vacuum. As Erbil grapples with deep internal divisions, Tehran is well positioned to make strategic gains.

The end of the US military mission in Iraq has created a dangerous security vacuum for the semi-autonomous Kurdish region.  

Politicians in Baghdad celebrated the withdrawal, with Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi officially declaring October 1 a "Day of Sovereignty and Independence."

Tehran, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), and Iranian-backed Shiite militias also cheered the move.

But in Erbil, the capital of Iraq's Kurdish region, the mood is markedly more anxious.

Having relied on Washington's protection for two decades, the Kurdistan Region of Iraq (KRI) now faces intertwined crises, including mounting pressure from Baghdad to centralize power and escalating military threats from its neighbors, most notably Iran.

A strategy of containment

The immediate threat to the Kurdistan region isn't a full-scale military invasion, but rather a slow, calculated chipping away of its autonomy, said Hesam Dastpish, a Middle East analyst based in Brussels.

He describes Tehran's overarching strategy toward Erbil as hostile and heavily focused on containment.

The Islamic Republic ultimately wants to strip the KRI of its political clout, reducing it to a purely administrative body, the expert stressed.

"Tehran's goal is to turn the Kurdistan region into an institution with absolutely no room to maneuver," Dastpish told DW, pointing to Iran's repeated strikes in the region, supposedly targeting camps of Iranian Kurdish opposition groups.

Salahuddin Khadiw, a political analyst based in Mahabad in Iran's Kurdish region, said that neighboring states don't necessarily want to wipe out Kurdish autonomy completely.

Instead, he underscored, Tehran envisions a "controlled and weak" Kurdistan.

By dealing separately with the rival power centers in Erbil and Sulaymaniyah, he argued, Iran has maintained influence across the KRI while seeking to prevent any single Kurdish authority from emerging as a dominant power on its western border.

Internal fragmentation remains a fatal flaw

Despite the external challenges, the Iraqi Kurdish region's most critical vulnerability comes from within.

The legacy of the 1990s civil war lives on through the deeply entrenched rivalry between the two main ruling factions: the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) and the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK).

Hiwa Mahmoud Osman, an analyst on Iraqi and Kurdish affairs in the Middle East, pointed out that Tehran leans heavily on this internal friction. "Iran has spent decades mastering political influence inside Iraq," he told DW. "The Kurds' biggest hurdle is their own fragmentation. Without a united front, foreign powers simply have more room to operate."

Ardeshir Pashang, a Middle East researcher in Tehran, warned that if Kurdish leaders fail to patch up their political quarrels, this disunity could ultimately lead to the collapse of the Kurdistan region as a political entity.

The opposition dilemma

A particularly thorny issue is the presence of Iranian Kurdish opposition outfits taking refuge in the KRI.

These groups, which have historically clashed with Iranian state forces, are now under immense pressure to disarm and relocate.

Their presence provides Iran with a convenient pretext to launch drone and missile strikes across the border, said Dastpish.

But he doesn't expect Erbil to offer "total surrender," as maintaining a balance with these groups is crucial for the KRI's domestic legitimacy and foreign relations.

Kasra Qaredaghi, a political science researcher based in the US, argues that these groups are now more vulnerable than ever.

If Iran was able to strike their sanctuaries while US forces were still fully deployed — culminating in a 2023 border security pact between Baghdad and Tehran — Erbil's leverage is now practically non-existent, giving Tehran significantly more power to force concessions, he said.

Dollar diplomacy is the United States' hidden weapon

While US troops may have left, Washington's leverage in Iraq has not entirely disappeared. It has simply transitioned toward global financial networks. Qaredaghi describes this as a "realignment of power," where the US, Turkey, and Saudi Arabia act as natural counterweights to Iran's growing reach.

Osman echoed this view, highlighting Iraq's deep financial reliance on the US dollar. This economic tether allows the US Treasury to indirectly influence Baghdad's internal affairs, right down to ensuring salaries are paid to KRI civil servants.

Khadiw similarly characterizes this strategic pivot as America transitioning from a "military balancer" to a "powerful economic observer."

But as internal and external pressures mount, the analysts said, Iraq's Kurdish region may have little choice but to heal its internal divides and present a united front to preserve its autonomy and limit Iran's strategic gains in the region.
